name: Olga Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My week is a mix of environmental science lectures, field trips to the river catchment, and a weekly data lab where we model rainfall. I live in a flat with my friend Dani above a bike shop. Weekends I teach maths online to two fourteen-year-olds for a tutoring site, and I do my reading while the kettle boils. I love the fieldwork. What wears me out is that I try to do everything, so I'm always eleven things behind.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being outside with a clipboard and then going home and making a model from the numbers. I use an AI assistant for every part of that, like tidying code and explaining stats I missed. What wears me out is money drifting away. My dad's an electrician and my mum translates documents, so they pay part of my rent, but mum's clients keep getting fewer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that gives us more time to fix actual problems, like the climate. Honestly I'd be a bit disappointed because I find the tools exciting. But I'd say it online with a shrug, because I'd still use them for what they do well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd still be uneasy, because even a small AI already bites at my mum's translation work. Machine translation is good enough that two of my mum's regular agencies now send her only the editing. If that's the plateau, it's still a slow squeeze for her, and I'd be helping with her rent share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with my degree and keep both tutoring students. I'd also work on a small project with my data lab tutor, because research assistants get paid a bit. And I'd teach my mum to use the best translation tools herself, so she charges for checking quality instead of fighting the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little flat, honestly. I'd feel safe in my own course but worried about home. It's like the weather is fine for me and rainy for Mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your mum take being taught by you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How would your mum take being taught by you?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the money side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd roll her eyes and say she's been translating since before I was born. Then she'd try it at night when nobody's watching. She's stubborn, but not silly. I'd sit with her on a Sunday and show her how to use it to check her drafts, and I'd tell her she's the expert and the tool is the intern.

say: I'd say it's good for **actual problems** like climate, though a bit disappointing for tool fans like me.
I'd shrug online: I'd still use the tools for what they **do well**.
think: Even a small AI already **bites** at my mum's translation work.
I feel safe in my degree but worried about **home**, like rain only on Mum.
do: **Keep** tutoring both students and working on my degree.
**Ask** my data lab tutor for a paid research assistant project.
**Teach** Mum to use translation tools to check her drafts.
feel: A little **flat**: the weather is fine for me and rainy for Mum.
S0.quote: Machine translation is good enough that two of my mum's regular agencies now send her only the editing.
fieldNote: Olga's **mood comes from home**, not her own course; her mum's shrinking work is already real.
She sees AI as a **tool she can teach**, which is why she plans to coach her mum.
She disguises worry with **humour** ('the tool is the intern').

steps.text: Ask my data lab tutor about a paid research assistant job
Teach Mum to use translation tools to check her drafts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the Steady Disruption picture is the one most likely to catch people off guard, because it's slow enough to ignore and fast enough to hurt. I'd put that on my feed with a link to retraining, because I'd rather be useful than loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be excited and worried at the same time. Environmental science uses data and writing, so some of it gets automated, and fieldwork and judgement remain. But my mum's translation work would shrink fast, and she'd need a new line of work by the time I graduate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get better at the tools that matter for my field, like data analysis and mapping. I'd also start a small project, like a map of the flood risk on our street, that I can show employers. And I'd find a course for Mum, maybe in language teaching, and pay for the first month myself from my tutoring money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Energised, and a little guilty about being excited when my mum's work is the thing being hit. I'd say the excitement and the worry feel like two flatmates who don't talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of those two flatmates wins in the end?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Which of those two flatmates wins in the end?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in that flood risk project?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The excited one, usually, because I can do something about it. The worried one wins at about two in the morning, when I'm doing the maths on how long Mum's savings last. Then I fall asleep and the excited one is back at breakfast making a to-do list. I think I need both.

say: I'd say this one **catches** people off guard: slow enough to ignore, fast enough to hurt.
I'd share a **retraining** link online, because I'd rather be useful than loud.
think: Some data and writing in my field gets automated, but **fieldwork** and judgement remain.
Mum's translation work would shrink **fast**, and she'd need new work by my graduation.
do: **Build** my skills in data analysis and mapping tools for environmental work.
**Make** a flood risk map of our street to show employers.
**Pay** the first month of a language-teaching course for Mum from tutoring money.
feel: **Energised** but guilty, since my excitement and my worry feel like flatmates who don't talk.
S1.quote: The Steady Disruption picture is the one most likely to catch people off guard, because it's slow enough to ignore and fast enough to hurt.
fieldNote: Mum's income pushes her to **anxious**: it is the household earner she expects to lose work.
Her **adaptive** side turns fear into projects; she builds a flood map to show employers.
The 'two flatmates' image shows she holds **excitement and worry** together.

steps.text: Practise mapping and data analysis tools every week
Build a flood risk map of our street
Pay for Mum's first month of a language teaching course
Take two more tutoring students for extra income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that this is a moment for the grown-ups to stop pretending. We'd need basic income pilots or something like it, and quickly. I'd also say that young people shouldn't be told to just upskill when the machine upskills faster than we do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm scared in a quiet way. By 2028 I'd be in my third year. Mum's translation work would be gone, and my degree's data and writing parts would be done by AI cheaper than me. Dad is an electrician, so he'd be safe until about 2031, but my family would live on one hands-on wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. I'd use my third year to build the physical side of my skills, like fieldwork and sampling, because robots need three more years. I'd take on more tutoring, save every spare pound, and talk to Mum and Dad about money honestly, with a spreadsheet. And I'd email my MP about basic income pilots, because someone has to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, buzzing and scared at once. My heart does a thing when I read the news. But I'd rather be moving than frozen, and I think I'd be moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the spreadsheet with your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would the spreadsheet with your parents say?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does basic income matter to you personally?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would say that Dad's wage covers the rent and food but not my share. I'd cut my own costs first, like dropping the gym and cooking in bulk. I'd also be honest that student debt isn't something I'm willing to take on for a degree that might not hold its value. If there's no job in 2029, I'd rather know now.

say: I'd say it's time for the grown-ups to **stop pretending** and try basic income pilots quickly.
I'd say young people shouldn't be told to **upskill** when machines upskill faster.
think: Mum's translation work would be **gone** and AI would do my degree's data parts cheaper.
Dad's wage as an electrician would carry the family until **2031**.
do: **Build** hands-on field skills in my third year, because robots need three more years.
**Take** more tutoring and save every spare pound.
**Email** my MP about basic income pilots and **share** a family budget with my parents.
feel: **Buzzing and scared**, but moving feels better than freezing.
S2.quote: Young people shouldn't be told to just upskill when the machine upskills faster than we do.
fieldNote: The **two-year clock** makes her treat the degree's value as uncertain, not only the job.
She actively **chooses movement** over fear: budgets, fieldwork, an email to her MP.
Her family's **single hands-on wage** is why the mood is anxious, not alarmed.

steps.text: Do extra fieldwork and sampling skills in the third year
Take two more tutoring students and save the pay
Email my MP about basic income pilots
Share a family budget spreadsheet with my parents

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years feels like enough time to build something good if we start now. I'd say that the tools should be taxed to pay for retraining, and I'd say it to my uni society and in my group chats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel hopeful, with a note of worry. I'd graduate in 2029 and have two years before anything big hits entry-level roles. Environmental fieldwork would survive the longest, and I'd aim for jobs that mix fieldwork and data, like flood modelling for councils. Mum's work would still be the problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a masters part-time if I could afford it, and I'd get a summer job with a council or a water company. I'd also keep using the AI tools to learn faster. I'd help Mum retrain into something like conference interpreting or teaching, where people still want a person. And I'd save about a quarter of my tutoring income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Optimistic, mostly. It feels like standing at the start of a long trail, with the weather unclear but the map decent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who thinks you're too relaxed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who thinks you're too relaxed?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your mum's retraining look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not relaxed, I'm just early. Being early is the only advantage I've got over people who are fifty, because I can try three things and fail at two. I'd tell them to start something small this month, even if it's only reading one course outline.

say: I'd say five years is **enough** to build something good if we start now.
I'd argue the tools should be **taxed** to pay for retraining, in my society and group chats.
think: I'd graduate in 2029 with **two years** before entry-level roles are hit.
Jobs mixing **fieldwork and data**, like flood modelling for councils, should last longest.
do: **Apply** for a summer job at a council or water company.
**Study** a part-time masters if I can afford it.
**Save** about a quarter of my tutoring income.
feel: **Hopeful**, like standing at the start of a trail with a decent map.
S3.quote: I'm not relaxed, I'm just early. Being early is the only advantage I've got over people who are fifty
fieldNote: Olga's **adaptiveness** is the main driver; five years lets her turn fear into a plan.
Mum's work remains the **sore spot**, keeping the mood at uneasy.
She treats her age as an **asset**, trying several things and accepting failure.

steps.text: Apply for a summer job with a council or water company
Save a quarter of my tutoring income
Help Mum look at interpreting or teaching courses
Study a part-time masters in flood modelling

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to get this right. I'd also say loudly that climate and AI should be planned together, because the power use of big AI systems matters and I'd want it written into rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'd feel mostly good. By 2036 I'd be twenty-nine, probably in a job I like and maybe even working on the climate side of AI. My parents would be about to retire, so the risk to them is smaller. I'd still worry that fewer people would get the chances I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree and aim for a job that uses fieldwork and models together. I'd try a few small side projects, like freelance data work, because I like the idea of earning money several ways. I'd also volunteer for a river group, so I'd have a network outside work. And I'd keep paying a little into a pension from my first job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cheerful, and a bit impatient. I'd want to start the exciting parts already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are you not saying about the people who don't have your chances?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What are you not saying about the people who don't have your chances?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a normal day look like for you in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the part that bugs me. I've got parents who can help and a good degree and a laptop. Someone who didn't get any of that wouldn't be able to try three things. So I'd want a lot of the money from the tools to go into free courses and good public libraries, and I'd say so.

say: I'd say ten years is a **real chance**, and climate and AI should be planned together.
I'd say the **power use** of big AI systems belongs in the rules.
think: By 2036 I'd be twenty-nine in a job I like, and my parents **near retirement**.
I'd worry that fewer people get the **chances** I've had.
do: **Aim** for a job combining fieldwork and models.
**Try** freelance data work as a second source of income.
**Volunteer** with a river group and pay into a pension from my first job.
feel: **Cheerful** and a bit impatient to start the exciting parts.
S4.quote: I've got parents who can help and a good degree and a laptop. Someone who didn't get any of that wouldn't be able to try three things.
fieldNote: With a decade, **Olga is calm** about herself and turns her worry outward to unequal chances.
She wants **side income streams**, a trait of her adaptive, curious style.
Her **fairness point** is concrete: free courses and good libraries.

steps.text: Aim for a first job that mixes fieldwork and modelling
Try freelance data work for small clients
Volunteer with a river conservation group
Pay into a pension from my first job

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, for sure. It would hit Mum's work, take away the safe path for my degree, and give nobody time to plan. What would help is quick retraining money, a basic income trial, and honest advice from universities on which skills last. Also, free access to good AI tools, so it isn't only the rich who can use them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd want people to know that young people who love these tools aren't naive about them. I use these tools every day, and that's exactly why I know how much they can change.

headlineQuote: I use these tools every day, and that's exactly why I know how much they can change.
portrait: Olga is **nineteen**, a first-year environmental science student who tutors maths online and shares a flat above a bike shop.
She is **progressive** and adaptive, using AI tools every day and treating change as something to build on.
Her mum's translation work is already shrinking, which keeps even calm worlds **uneasy** at home.
She turns fear into **projects**, such as a flood map, tutoring and emails to her MP, and fears inequality.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most: it hits Mum's work and her degree's value, with no time to plan.
whatWouldHelp: Quick **retraining money**, a basic income trial and free access to good AI tools for everyone.
